jurisdiction.name: United Kingdom
jurisdiction.overview: Nationally published records appear separately from applicable EU-level records. The landscape, historical relationships and legal applicability remain under document-level review.

narrative.summary: The United Kingdom has no AI-specific statute and regulates AI through existing law and sector regulators, following the principles-based approach set in the 2023 AI regulation white paper and the government's February 2024 response. The main binding rules are in data protection law, where the Data (Use and Access) Act 2025 rewrote the rules on automated decision-making from February 2026 and requires an ICO code of practice on AI; in the Online Safety Act 2023 and the Crime and Policing Act 2026, which create offences around deepfakes and AI image generators; and in the Automated Vehicles Act 2024. Government policy is led by DSIT through the AI Opportunities Action Plan (2025), with the AI Security Institute testing frontier models and the Cabinet Office's AI Playbook and Algorithmic Transparency Recording Standard governing public-sector use. Regulators including the ICO (now the Information Commission), CMA, FCA, Bank of England, Ofcom, MHRA and EHRC publish their own AI approaches, and the CMA has imposed a binding conduct requirement on Google's use of publisher content in generative AI. Scotland and Wales have their own AI strategies and Northern Ireland is consulting on its first.
lead_institutions: Department for Science, Innovation and Technology
Information Commission (formerly the Information Commissioner's Office)
Financial Conduct Authority and Bank of England / PRA
Medicines and Healthcare products Regulatory Agency
Scottish Government, Welsh Government and Northern Ireland Executive
narrative.review_notes: Deep review completed on 7 October 2026, covering UK-wide legislation, central government (DSIT, the AI Security Institute, the Cabinet Office and Government Digital Service, NCSC and policy departments), the main regulators (ICO, CMA, FCA, Bank of England, Ofcom, MHRA, EHRC and the Digital Regulation Cooperation Forum), the Scottish, Welsh and Northern Ireland governments, and the Greater London Authority and other large cities. The Ofcom, Equality and Human Rights Commission and Digital Regulation Cooperation Forum websites could not be read automatically, so their documents were checked against archived copies of the official pages; several city council websites could not be read either. Pending: the ICO statutory code on AI and automated decision-making, Northern Ireland's final AI strategy, AI updates from other regulators (such as Ofgem, Ofqual and the HSE), defence AI policy, and AI policies of other councils. Jersey, Guernsey, the Isle of Man, Gibraltar and other Crown Dependencies and Overseas Territories are separate jurisdictions; no AI documents from them came up in this review.

instruments.official_title: Guidelines for AI procurement
instruments.english_title: Guidelines for AI procurement
instruments.current_status: Published 8 June 2020 by the Office for Artificial Intelligence (page now tagged to DSIT, the former DCMS and BEIS); not withdrawn or updated since. Non-binding guidance; later central-government AI buying guidance is in the AI Playbook (2025) and PPN 017.
instruments.summary: Sets out ten 'top considerations' and a summary of best practice for public-sector buyers acquiring AI, from embedding procurement in an AI adoption strategy and data assessment through to multidisciplinary teams, problem-focused specifications, ethics and lifecycle governance; it was initiated through the World Economic Forum's 'Unlocking public sector AI' project. Aimed at central government buyers and other public bodies; it complements the Data Ethics Framework and the 2019 'Guide to using AI in the public sector'.
instruments.ai_governance_relevance: UK central-government instrument shaping AI governance (procurement, public-sector).

instruments.official_title: PPN 017: Improving transparency of AI use in procurement
instruments.english_title: PPN 017: Improving transparency of AI use in procurement
instruments.current_status: Issued 17 February 2025 by the Cabinet Office; applies to procurements commenced on or after 24 February 2025 under the Procurement Act 2023 (PPN 02/24 continues to apply to procurements commenced before that date). The disclosure questions are optional; other public bodies may apply the approach.
instruments.summary: Procurement Policy Note for central government departments, executive agencies and NDPBs giving optional questions contracting authorities can use to ask suppliers to disclose their use of AI in bids and in delivering services, and advising on the risks of AI-generated tender content. It updates PPN 02/24 to Procurement Act 2023 terminology and applies to procurements commenced on or after 24 February 2025.
instruments.ai_governance_relevance: UK central-government instrument shaping AI governance (procurement, transparency, public-sector).

instruments.official_title: AI Playbook for the UK Government
instruments.english_title: AI Playbook for the UK Government
instruments.current_status: Published 10 February 2025 by GDS (ISBN 9781036688745); current. Replaced the Generative AI Framework for HMG, which gov.uk marks withdrawn on 10 February 2025. Supplemented by the AI Insights technical series.
instruments.summary: Guidance for civil servants and people working in government organisations on using AI safely, effectively and securely, built around 10 principles (e.g. know what AI is and its limits, use it lawfully and ethically, keep meaningful human control, work with commercial colleagues). It explains AI capabilities and risks and how to select, buy and deploy AI, and expands and retitles the January 2024 Generative AI Framework for HMG to cover a wider range of AI technologies.
instruments.ai_governance_relevance: UK central-government instrument shaping AI governance (public-sector, generative-ai, government-governance, procurement).

instruments.official_title: Data and AI Ethics Framework
instruments.english_title: Data and AI Ethics Framework
instruments.current_status: Current version published 18 December 2025, when the 2020 Data Ethics Framework (first issued 13 June 2018) was retitled the Data and AI Ethics Framework, extended to AI and algorithmic tools and given 4 new principles. Non-binding guidance for public servants.
instruments.summary: Principles and recommended actions to guide the responsible development, procurement and use of data and AI in the public sector, organised around seven principles: transparency, accountability, fairness, privacy, environmental sustainability, societal impact and safety. Teams working on AI or data-driven projects are told to use it with the accompanying Data and AI Ethics Self-Assessment Tool.
instruments.ai_governance_relevance: UK central-government instrument shaping AI governance (ethics, public-sector).

instruments.official_title: Algorithmic Transparency Recording Standard Mandatory Scope and Exemptions Policy
instruments.english_title: Algorithmic Transparency Recording Standard Mandatory Scope and Exemptions Policy
instruments.current_status: Published 17 December 2024 by GDS. Implements the mandate across government departments announced in the 6 February 2024 government response to the AI regulation white paper, with a stated intent to extend it to the wider public sector over time.
instruments.summary: Defines which organisations and algorithmic tools fall within the mandatory requirement to publish Algorithmic Transparency Recording Standard (ATRS) records: ministerial and non-ministerial departments and arm's-length bodies that provide public or frontline services or routinely interact with the public, for tools with significant influence on decisions with public effect or that interact directly with the public. It also sets out exemptions and the steps for handling sensitive information before publication.
instruments.ai_governance_relevance: UK central-government instrument shaping AI governance (transparency, public-sector).

instruments.official_title: Algorithmic Transparency Recording Standard - guidance for public sector bodies
instruments.english_title: Algorithmic Transparency Recording Standard - guidance for public sector bodies
instruments.current_status: First published 5 January 2023; guidance updated 8 May 2025 alongside a new ATRS template version. Hosted on the publication page 'Guidance for organisations using the Algorithmic Transparency Recording Standard'.
instruments.summary: Step-by-step guidance for public sector teams completing the ATRS template and publishing completed records to the GOV.UK repository, covering the Tier 1 summary and Tier 2 detailed information about an algorithmic tool, its owners, data, risks and impact assessments. It applies both to central government bodies required to publish under the mandatory policy and to organisations publishing voluntarily.
instruments.ai_governance_relevance: UK central-government instrument shaping AI governance (transparency, public-sector).

instruments.official_title: Guidelines for secure AI system development
instruments.english_title: Guidelines for secure AI system development
instruments.current_status: Published 27 November 2023 on ncsc.gov.uk with PDF; current. Non-binding. The DSIT Code of Practice for the Cyber Security of AI (January 2025) builds on these guidelines.
instruments.summary: Guidelines for providers of any system that uses AI, whether built from scratch or on top of third-party tools, organised around four lifecycle stages: secure design, secure development, secure deployment, and secure operation and maintenance. Published by the NCSC and the US CISA with international partner agencies (including NSA, FBI and the Australian, Canadian, New Zealand and other national cyber agencies).
instruments.ai_governance_relevance: UK central-government instrument shaping AI governance (cyber-security).

instruments.official_title: Guidance on AI and data protection
instruments.english_title: Guidance on AI and data protection
instruments.current_status: Current version dated 15 March 2023 on the ICO page (the guidance was first published earlier; the ICO page gives no original date). The ICO states the guidance is under review because of changes made by the Data (Use and Access) Act 2025. Functions of the Information Commissioner passed to the Information Commission on 30 September 2026 (DUAA 2025 ss.118-119; SI 2026/1015); the guidance remains on ico.org.uk.
instruments.summary: Detailed ICO guidance on applying UK GDPR principles to AI systems, organised by principle: accountability and governance (including DPIAs), transparency, lawfulness (inferences, affinity groups, special category data), accuracy and statistical accuracy, fairness, security and data minimisation, and individual rights. The March 2023 update added a fairness chapter and an annex on fairness across the AI lifecycle, covering bias mitigation, processing personal data for bias detection and the link between solely automated decisions and Article 22 safeguards.
instruments.ai_governance_relevance: Regulator-level primary source (Information Commissioner's Office) for data-privacy, risk-assurance, transparency.
metadata_gaps: Original first-publication date not stated on the official page; publication_date records the current version date (15 March 2023)

instruments.official_title: National AI Strategy
instruments.english_title: National AI Strategy
instruments.issuing_authority: HM Government (Office for Artificial Intelligence; Department for Digital, Culture, Media & Sport; Department for Business, Energy & Industrial Strategy)
instruments.publisher_name: HM Government (Office for Artificial Intelligence; Department for Digital, Culture, Media & Sport; Department for Business, Energy & Industrial Strategy)
instruments.current_status: Published 22 September 2021; updated 18 December 2022 with an infographic of 2022 achievements. Not withdrawn on gov.uk and no official statement of supersession found; the government's current AI plan is the AI Opportunities Action Plan (January 2025).
instruments.summary: The UK's ten-year plan to make Britain a 'global AI superpower', built on three pillars: investing in the long-term needs of the AI ecosystem, ensuring AI benefits all sectors and regions, and governing AI effectively. It committed the government to developing a pro-innovation national position on governing and regulating AI, which led to the 2022 policy paper and the 2023 white paper.
instruments.ai_governance_relevance: UK central-government instrument shaping AI governance (strategy).

instruments.official_title: AI Opportunities Action Plan: One Year On
instruments.english_title: AI Opportunities Action Plan: One Year On
instruments.issuing_authority: Department for Science, Innovation and Technology
instruments.publisher_name: Department for Science, Innovation and Technology
instruments.current_status: Published 29 January 2026 by DSIT (HTML and 16-page PDF).
instruments.summary: Progress report on the AI Opportunities Action Plan stating that the government has met 38 of the plan's 50 actions in its first year, with updates across three priorities: laying the foundations to enable AI, changing lives by embracing AI, and securing the UK's future with homegrown AI. Detailed per-action progress is published in a companion AI Opportunities Action Plan dashboard.
instruments.ai_governance_relevance: UK central-government instrument shaping AI governance (strategy).

instruments.official_title: Code of Practice for the Cyber Security of AI
instruments.english_title: Code of Practice for the Cyber Security of AI (AI Cyber Security Code of Practice)
instruments.issuing_authority: Department for Science, Innovation and Technology
instruments.publisher_name: Department for Science, Innovation and Technology
instruments.current_status: Published 31 January 2025 by DSIT (developed with the NCSC) after a 2024 call for views, together with an implementation guide. Voluntary. The gov.uk page is now also tagged to the Department for Digital, Culture, Media and Sport created in July 2026.
instruments.summary: Voluntary code setting 13 baseline cyber security principles for AI systems across five lifecycle phases (secure design, development, deployment, maintenance and end of life), addressing AI-specific risks such as data poisoning, model obfuscation and indirect prompt injection. It applies to developers, system operators and data custodians, and forms the first part of a two-part intervention to create a global baseline standard in ETSI.
instruments.ai_governance_relevance: UK central-government instrument shaping AI governance (cyber-security).

instruments.official_title: Data Protection Act 2018
instruments.english_title: Data Protection Act 2018 and UK GDPR (automated decision-making framework)
instruments.current_status: Royal Assent 23 May 2018; main provisions in force 25 May 2018 (SI 2018/625). Read with the UK GDPR (retained Regulation (EU) 2016/679). The original automated-decision rules (UK GDPR Art. 22, DPA 2018 ss.14, 49-50) were replaced by UK GDPR Arts. 22A-22D and DPA 2018 ss.50A-50D, inserted by Data (Use and Access) Act 2025 s.80, in force 5 February 2026 (SI 2026/82, reg. 2(j)); decisions taken before that date stay under the old rules (reg. 5). Intelligence-services ADM rules (ss.96-97) amended by the same section. In force as amended.
instruments.summary: The UK's general data protection framework: the Data Protection Act 2018 together with the UK GDPR governs processing of personal data, including for training and using AI systems, and is enforced by the Information Commissioner. Since 5 February 2026 its automated decision-making rules are UK GDPR Arts. 22A-22D (general processing) and DPA 2018 ss.50A-50D (law enforcement): significant decisions based solely on automated processing are restricted only where they use special category data or rely on recognised legitimate interests, and controllers must provide safeguards letting people get information, make representations, obtain human intervention and contest the decision. Part 4 (ss.96-97) separately governs automated decisions by the intelligence services.
instruments.ai_governance_relevance: Horizontal data protection law that governs AI training and use of personal data and sets the UK rules on solely automated decision-making and profiling.

instruments.official_title: Data (Use and Access) Act 2025
instruments.english_title: Data (Use and Access) Act 2025
instruments.current_status: Royal Assent 19 June 2025; commenced in stages by regulations under s.142 (nine commencement SIs to September 2026). Copyright and AI duties ss.135-137 in force 20 August 2025 (SI 2025/904); s.80 automated decision-making in force 5 February 2026 (SI 2026/82, Commencement No. 6, with a saving for pre-commencement decisions); s.138 purported intimate image offences in force 6 February 2026 (SI 2026/31, Commencement No. 5); ss.118-119 replace the Information Commissioner with the Information Commission from 30 September 2026 (SI 2026/1015). No regulations under UK GDPR Art. 22D or DPA 2018 s.50D found on legislation.gov.uk as of 7 October 2026.
instruments.summary: Wide-ranging data reform Act that, in s.80 and Sch. 6, replaces UK GDPR Art. 22 and DPA 2018 ss.49-50 with new automated decision-making rules (Arts. 22A-22D, ss.50A-50D): 'meaningful human involvement' defines a solely automated decision, restrictions now apply mainly to decisions using special category data, and every significant automated decision needs safeguards (information, representations, human intervention, contest), with powers for the Secretary of State to set further rules by affirmative regulations. Sections 135-137 required the Government to publish a copyright and AI economic impact assessment and report within nine months (with a statutory definition of 'AI system'), and s.138 inserts ss.66E-66H into the Sexual Offences Act 2003, creating offences of creating, or requesting the creation of, a purported intimate image (deepfake) of an adult without consent. It also lets regulations require Information Commissioner codes of practice (new DPA 2018 ss.124A-124B).
instruments.ai_governance_relevance: Primary legislation reforming UK rules on automated decision-making, mandating government work on copyright and AI, and criminalising the creation of sexually explicit deepfakes.

instruments.official_title: The Data Protection Act 2018 (Code of Practice on Artificial Intelligence and Automated Decision-Making) Regulations 2026
instruments.english_title: The Data Protection Act 2018 (Code of Practice on Artificial Intelligence and Automated Decision-Making) Regulations 2026
instruments.issuing_authority: Department for Science, Innovation and Technology
instruments.current_status: Made 16 April 2026 by Ian Murray, Minister of State, DSIT; laid 21 April 2026; in force 12 May 2026 (21 days after laying). Extends to the whole UK. In force; the code it requires had not been checked under this part (regulator guidance is reviewed separately).
instruments.summary: Statutory instrument made under DPA 2018 ss.124A and 124B that requires the Information Commissioner to prepare a code of practice giving guidance on good practice in processing personal data when developing and using artificial intelligence and in automated decision-making (as defined by UK GDPR Art. 22C(1) and DPA 2018 s.50C(1)). The code must include guidance on processing children's personal data and covers the UK GDPR and DPA 2018 except Part 4; the review panel the Commissioner must set up may not consider national security aspects.
instruments.ai_governance_relevance: AI-specific secondary legislation creating the legal duty for a statutory ICO code of practice on AI and automated decision-making.

instruments.official_title: Online Safety Act 2023
instruments.english_title: Online Safety Act 2023
instruments.current_status: Royal Assent 26 October 2023; commenced in stages (Commencement No. 1-7 regulations to April 2026); ss.55 and 231 in force at Royal Assent; s.188 (intimate image offences, including computer-generated images) in force 31 January 2024 (SI 2024/31). SI 2025/1352 made the s.66B intimate image sharing offence a priority offence from 8 January 2026. Section 216A (power to extend the Act to illegal AI-generated content and AI services) inserted by Crime and Policing Act 2026 s.248 from 29 April 2026; no regulations under it found as of 7 October 2026 (a progress report is due by 31 December 2026 under that Act's s.249). In force as amended.
instruments.summary: Ofcom-enforced online safety regime imposing illegal-content and child-safety duties on user-to-user and search services. Content generated by bots or automated tools counts as user-generated content where the tool is not controlled by the provider (s.55(4)), bot-generated content can amount to illegal content (s.59(12), s.192(7)), and 'proactive technology' expressly includes AI and machine-learning tools (s.231(10)); s.188 created the Sexual Offences Act 2003 s.66B offence of sharing intimate images, which covers images made or altered by computer graphics. Since April 2026 s.216A lets the Secretary of State, by regulations, impose illegal-content, CSEA-reporting and fraudulent-advertising duties on providers of AI services that generate content and extend Ofcom's powers to them.
instruments.ai_governance_relevance: Main UK online safety statute; applies to AI-generated content on regulated services and now carries a specific power to regulate generative AI services.

instruments.official_title: Crime and Policing Act 2026
instruments.english_title: Crime and Policing Act 2026
instruments.current_status: Royal Assent 29 April 2026. Section 248 (new Online Safety Act s.216A) and s.249 in force at Royal Assent (s.255(2)(k)). Section 99 (purported intimate image generators) in force 29 June 2026 (SI 2026/689, Commencement No. 1). Sections 72-76 (CSA image-generators and CSA image guidance offences) not yet in force as of 7 October 2026 (England and Wales by Home Office regulations; Northern Ireland and Scotland by the devolved authorities under s.255(8) and (10)). Partly in force.
instruments.summary: Omnibus criminal justice Act with several AI-specific provisions. Sections 72-74 create offences (up to 5 years) of making, adapting, possessing or supplying a 'CSA image-generator' - any program, electronic information or service made or adapted to create child sexual abuse images - in each UK jurisdiction, with ss.75-76 covering possession of guidance on creating such images; s.99 inserts Sexual Offences Act 2003 ss.66I-66K, making it an offence (up to 3 years) to make, adapt, supply or offer a tool for creating purported intimate (deepfake) images, with a reasonable-steps defence. Section 248 gives the Secretary of State power to extend the Online Safety Act 2023 to illegal AI-generated content and AI services, and s.249 requires a progress report to Parliament by 31 December 2026 unless draft regulations are laid first.
instruments.ai_governance_relevance: Criminalises AI tools built to generate child sexual abuse images or non-consensual intimate deepfakes, and creates the power to regulate AI chatbots and generators under the Online Safety Act.

instruments.official_title: Automated Vehicles Act 2024
instruments.english_title: Automated Vehicles Act 2024
instruments.current_status: Royal Assent 20 May 2024; most of Part 1 (authorisation, self-driving test, statement of safety principles) not yet in force. Commencement: ss.55-56 and regulation-making powers in ss.78, 88-89 from 1 January 2026 (SI 2025/1339); Part 5 permits for automated passenger services (except s.84 civil sanctions) from 15 May 2026 (SI 2026/437); Part 4 marketing restrictions from 7 January 2027 (SI 2026/731). Partly in force.
instruments.scope: Great Britain (most provisions extend to England and Wales and Scotland)
instruments.summary: Framework law for self-driving vehicles in Great Britain: a vehicle may be authorised only if it meets a 'self-driving test' (it can travel autonomously, safely and legally), assessed against a statement of safety principles that must aim for safety at least equal to careful and competent human drivers and be approved by Parliament. It makes authorised self-driving entities and no-user-in-charge operators responsible for vehicle conduct, gives the user-in-charge immunity for the manner of driving, creates information duties, offences and sanctions, restricts marketing terms such as 'self-driving' to authorised vehicles (Part 4), and sets up a permit scheme for automated passenger services (Part 5).
instruments.ai_governance_relevance: Sector-specific statute regulating the safety, authorisation, liability and marketing of AI-driven automated vehicles.
metadata_gaps: Act as a whole has no single commencement date; effective_date is the first commencement (1 January 2026, SI 2025/1339)

instruments.official_title: The Automated Vehicles (Permits for Automated Passenger Services) Regulations 2026
instruments.english_title: The Automated Vehicles (Permits for Automated Passenger Services) Regulations 2026
instruments.current_status: Made 20 April 2026; laid 23 April 2026; in force 15 May 2026, the same day Part 5 of the Automated Vehicles Act 2024 was commenced (SI 2026/437). In force.
instruments.scope: England, Wales and Scotland (bus-like services); England (taxi- and private-hire-like services)
instruments.summary: Procedural regulations under Automated Vehicles Act 2024 ss.88-89 that make the permit scheme for automated passenger services work: permits last at most five years, may be renewed in a window between six and two months before expiry, and may be varied, suspended or withdrawn by the Secretary of State with or without the holder's consent (including an urgent procedure). They also provide internal review of decisions and permit disclosure of information for specified purposes, applying to bus-like services in Great Britain and taxi- and private-hire-like services in England.
instruments.ai_governance_relevance: Secondary legislation enabling permits for passenger services in self-driving vehicles.

instruments.official_title: The Automated Vehicles (Marketing Restrictions) Regulations 2026
instruments.english_title: The Automated Vehicles (Marketing Restrictions) Regulations 2026
instruments.current_status: Made 1 July 2026; laid 7 July 2026; comes into force 7 January 2027, alongside Part 4 of the Automated Vehicles Act 2024 (SI 2026/731). Made, not yet in force.
instruments.summary: Regulations under Automated Vehicles Act 2024 s.78 listing the 'restricted terms' that may be used to promote or supply a road vehicle or vehicle equipment only if the vehicle is an authorised automated vehicle: 'automated', 'automated driving', 'autonomous', 'autonomous driving', 'drive autonomously', 'drive itself', 'driverless' and 'self-driving' (and their grammatical variants). 'Automated' and 'autonomous' are restricted only when describing a vehicle as a whole or its overall driving capability; misuse is an offence under s.78.
instruments.ai_governance_relevance: Restricts marketing claims that a vehicle is self-driving to vehicles authorised under the AV safety regime.

instruments.official_title: Automated and Electric Vehicles Act 2018
instruments.english_title: Automated and Electric Vehicles Act 2018
instruments.current_status: Royal Assent 19 July 2018; Part 1 (ss.1-8, automated vehicles: liability of insurers) in force 21 April 2021 (SI 2021/396). The Road Vehicles (Construction and Use) (Automated Vehicles) Order 2022 (SI 2022/470, in force 1 July 2022) relies on its definition to let drivers view built-in screens while a listed vehicle is driving itself. In force; Automated Vehicles Act 2024 provides the newer authorisation regime.
instruments.scope: Great Britain (Part 1 extends to England and Wales and Scotland)
instruments.summary: Part 1 sets the liability rules for accidents caused by automated vehicles: the Secretary of State keeps a list of vehicles capable of safely driving themselves, and where such a vehicle causes an accident while driving itself the insurer (or the owner, if uninsured and exempt) is directly liable to injured parties, with limited exclusions for unauthorised software alterations or failure to install safety-critical updates. Part 2 concerns electric-vehicle charging and is not AI-related.
instruments.ai_governance_relevance: Earlier UK statute allocating insurance liability for self-driving vehicles.

instruments.official_title: Copyright, Designs and Patents Act 1988
instruments.english_title: Copyright, Designs and Patents Act 1988 (s.9(3) computer-generated works)
instruments.current_status: Royal Assent 15 November 1988. Sections 9(3), 12(7) and 178 ('computer-generated') remain in force unamended as of 7 October 2026. The Government's March 2026 Report on Copyright and Artificial Intelligence proposes that this specific protection for computer-generated works be removed; no amending legislation found.
instruments.summary: The UK copyright statute, relevant to AI because it protects 'computer-generated' works, defined in s.178 as works generated by computer where there is no human author. For such literary, dramatic, musical or artistic works the author is taken to be the person who made the arrangements necessary for their creation (s.9(3)), and copyright lasts 50 years from the end of the year of making (s.12(7)). Its general rules also govern whether copying works to train AI models infringes copyright, the subject of the 2024-2026 copyright and AI review.
instruments.ai_governance_relevance: Statutory basis for copyright in AI-generated output and for the rules on using copyright works to train AI.
metadata_gaps: Act commenced in stages from 1 August 1989; date for s.9(3) not separately recorded here

instruments.official_title: The National Security and Investment Act 2021 (Notifiable Acquisition) (Specification of Qualifying Entities) Regulations 2021
instruments.english_title: The National Security and Investment Act 2021 (Notifiable Acquisition) (Specification of Qualifying Entities) Regulations 2021
instruments.issuing_authority: Department for Business, Energy and Industrial Strategy
instruments.current_status: Made 10 November 2021 (Lord Callanan, BEIS) after affirmative approval; in force 4 January 2022. Schedule 3 (artificial intelligence) unamended per legislation.gov.uk as of 7 October 2026. In force.
instruments.summary: Regulations under the National Security and Investment Act 2021 defining the 17 sensitive areas in which acquisitions of control must be notified to and approved by the Secretary of State before completion. Schedule 3 defines 'artificial intelligence' and captures entities that research AI or develop or produce goods, software or technology using AI for identifying or tracking objects, people or events, advanced robotics or cyber security. Under the 2021 Act, a notifiable acquisition completed without the Secretary of State's approval is void.
instruments.ai_governance_relevance: Binding regulation that makes AI one of the sectors subject to mandatory national-security screening of investments.

instruments.official_title: Report and impact assessment on Copyright and Artificial Intelligence
instruments.english_title: Report and impact assessment on Copyright and Artificial Intelligence
instruments.issuing_authority: Department for Science, Innovation and Technology; Department for Culture, Media and Sport; Intellectual Property Office
instruments.current_status: Published 18 March 2026 and laid before Parliament under Data (Use and Access) Act 2025 ss.135-136 (report CP 2602959 with economic impact assessment). Preceded by the s.137 progress statement of 15 December 2025. Sets the current government position; no legislation proposed yet.
instruments.summary: Statutory report and economic impact assessment on the use of copyright works to develop AI systems, responding to the December 2024 consultation (11,520 responses). The Government states that a broad text-and-data-mining exception with opt-out is no longer its preferred way forward, that it will not reform copyright law until confident reforms meet its objectives, and that it will gather further evidence while encouraging transparency, technical standards and licensing. It also proposes removing the specific protection for computer-generated works (CDPA s.9(3)) and discusses gaps in protection against unauthorised digital replicas (deepfakes).
instruments.ai_governance_relevance: Government's statutory policy position on AI training and copyright, computer-generated works and digital replicas.

instruments.official_title: Copyright and Artificial Intelligence

Council sites that blocked automated access: cardiff.gov.uk and cardiff.moderngov.co.uk, glasgow.gov.uk, Liverpool City Region Combined Authority, camden.gov.uk; the london.gov.uk taskforce page (report read from the official PDF). GMCA policy is sourced from GMCA's committee-document system on civico.net. legislation.gov.uk full-text search returned no AI hits in Acts of the Scottish Parliament, Senedd or NI Assembly; its index may not cover every recent instrument. Information Commissioner abolished and functions transferred to the Information Commission on 30 September 2026 (DUAA ss.118-119, SI 2026/1015 reg 2); earlier ICO documents keep the ICO as issuer. No part of this run was interrupted, so no record was written before a restart; the 14 pre-existing records were re-checked against their official pages by the central-government and regulators parts.
